children.translated_text: The <s>Kāvyālaṅkāra-sūtras</s> with commentary composed by the eminent scholar <s>Śrī Vāmana</s>
Now, the first chapter of the first section.
Having bowed to the Supreme Light, by <s>Vāmana</s>, dear to poets,
the commentary on those <s>Kāvyālaṅkāra-sūtras</s> is composed.
Poetry is to be valued on account of <s>alaṅkāra</s> (ornamentation). // VKal_1,1.1 //

children.text: kāvyaṃ khalu grāhyamupādeyaṃ bhavati, alaṅkārāt / kāvyaśabdo'yaṃ guṇālaṅkārasaṃskṛtayoḥ śabdārthayorvartate / bhaktyā tu śabdārthamātravacano'tra gṛhyate //1//
children.translated_text: Poetry indeed is to be valued, that is, worthy of acceptance, on account of <s>alaṅkāra</s> (ornamentation). The word 'poetry' here refers to word and meaning embellished by <s>guṇas</s> (qualities) and <s>alaṅkāras</s> (ornaments). However, in a secondary sense, it is taken here as referring merely to word and meaning. //1//
What then is this <s>alaṅkāra</s>? To this he says —
Beauty is <s>alaṅkāra</s> (ornamentation). // VKal_1,1.2 //
Embellishment is <s>alaṅkāra</s>. However, by etymological derivation from the instrumental sense, the word <s>alaṅkāra</s> applies to <s>upamā</s> (simile) and other [figures]. //2//
That [beauty] is [achieved] through the avoidance of <s>doṣas</s> (faults) and the adoption of <s>guṇas</s> (qualities) and <s>alaṅkāras</s> (ornaments). // VKal_1,1.3 //

children.text: sa khalvalaṅkāro doṣahānād guṇālaṅkārādānācc sampādyaḥ kaveḥ //3//
children.translated_text: That <s>alaṅkāra</s> (beauty) indeed is to be accomplished by the poet through the avoidance of faults and the adoption of qualities and ornaments. //3//
These [are known] from this treatise. // VKal_1,1.4 //

children.text: te doṣaguṇālaṅkārahānādāne / śāstrādasmāt / śāstrato hi jñātvā doṣāñjahyād , guṇālaṅkārāṃścādadīta //4//
children.translated_text: These — the avoidance of faults and adoption of qualities and ornaments — [are known] from this treatise. For, having known from this treatise, one should abandon faults and adopt qualities and ornaments. //4//

children.text: kiṃ punaḥ phalam alaṅkaravatā kāvyena, yenaitadartho'yamityāha ----
children.translated_text: Now, what is the purpose of poetry possessing ornamentation, that this [treatise] is devoted to it? To this he says —
Good poetry serves both visible and invisible purposes, because it is the cause of pleasure and fame. // VKal_1,1.5 //

children.text: {kāvyaṃ sat} cāru dṛṣṭaprayojanaṃ , prītihetutvāt / adṛṣṭaprayojanaṃ kīrtihetutvāt / atra ślokāḥ ----
children.translated_text: Good poetry — that is, beautiful [poetry] — has a visible purpose, because it is the cause of pleasure; and an invisible purpose, because it is the cause of fame. Here are [illustrative] verses —
They regard the composition of poetry as the foundation,
as the pathway to fame; but the mockery of bad poetry as the path of infamy.
The wise declare fame to have heaven as its fruit, in perpetuity,
but infamy to be the messenger sent to the region of the lightless hell.

children.text:
tasmāt kīrtimupādātumakīrtiṃ ca nivarhitum /
  kāvyālaṅkārasūtrārthaḥ prasādyaḥ kavipuṅgavaiḥ //
children.translated_text:
Therefore, to acquire fame and to ward off infamy,
the meaning of the <s>Kāvyālaṅkāra-sūtras</s> should be mastered by the foremost of poets.

children.text: iti śrīpaṇḍitavaravāmanaviracitakāvyālaṅkārasūtravṛttau śarīre prathame'dhikaraṇe prathamo'dhyāyaḥ iti prayojanasthāpanā //1-1//
children.translated_text: Thus ends the first chapter of the first section on the body in the commentary on the <s>Kāvyālaṅkāra-sūtras</s> composed by the eminent scholar <s>Vāmana</s>. This is the establishment of the purpose. //1-1//
Now, the second chapter of the first section.
Establishment of purpose.
For the purpose of determining the qualified student, he says —
Poets are of two kinds: the discerning (<s>arocakin</s>) and the indiscriminate (<s>satṛṇābhyavahārin</s>). // VKal_1,2.1 //

children.text: iha khalu dvaye kavayaḥ sambhavanti / arocakinaḥ , satṛṇābhyavahāriṇaśceti / arocakisatṛṇābhyavahāriśabdau gauṇārthau / ko'sāvarthaḥ / vivekitvamavivekitvaṃ ceti //1//
children.translated_text: Here, poets are of two kinds: the discerning and the indiscriminate. The words <s>arocakin</s> and <s>satṛṇābhyavahārin</s> are used in a figurative sense. What is that meaning? Discrimination and lack of discrimination respectively. //1//
As he says —
The former are [fit] students, because of their discrimination. // VKal_1,2.2 //

children.text: pūrve khalvarocakinaḥ śiṣyāḥ śāsanīyāḥ / vivekitvāt vivecanaśīlatvāt //2//
children.translated_text: The former, the discerning ones, are students — that is, fit to be instructed — because of their discrimination, their habit of discernment. //2//
Not the others, because of the opposite of that. // VKal_1,2.3 //

children.text: itare satṛṇābhyavahāriṇo na śiṣyāḥ / tadviparyayāt / avivecanaśīlatvāt / na ca śīlamapākartuṃ śakyam //3//
children.translated_text: The others, the indiscriminate ones, are not [fit] students, because of the opposite of that — because of their lack of the habit of discernment. And a natural disposition cannot be removed. //3//

children.text: nanvevaṃ na śāstraṃ sarvatrānugrāhi syāt , ko vā manyate , tadāha ----
children.translated_text: Then would the treatise not benefit everyone? Or does anyone think so? To this he says —
A treatise is not effective for unworthy persons. // VKal_1,2.4 //
A treatise is indeed not effective for the unworthy, the undiscriminating. //4//
He gives an illustration —
The clearing-nut is not for the clarification of mud. // VKal_1,2.5 //

children.text: na hi katakaṃ payasa iva pañkaprasādanāya bhavati //5//
children.translated_text: The <s>kataka</s> (clearing-nut) does not serve to clarify mud, as it does water. //5//
Having determined the qualified student, for the purpose of ascertaining <s>rīti</s> (style), he says —
<s>Rīti</s> (style) is the soul of poetry. // VKal_1,2.6 //
This thing called <s>rīti</s> is the soul of poetry — as of the body, this being the completion of the statement. //6//
What then is this <s>rīti</s>? To this he says —
A distinctive arrangement of words is <s>rīti</s> (style). // VKal_1,2.7 //
A composition of words possessing distinction is <s>rīti</s> (style). //7//
What is that distinction? To this he says —
The distinction consists of <s>guṇas</s> (qualities). // VKal_1,2.8 //
The distinction is of the nature of the <s>guṇas</s> (qualities) which will be described. //8//

children.text: sā tridhā vaidarbhī gauḍīyā pāñcālī ceti // VKal_1,2.9 //
children.translated_text: It [<s>rīti</s>] is of three kinds: <s>Vaidarbhī</s>, <s>Gauḍīyā</s>, and <s>Pāñcālī</s>. // VKal_1,2.9 //

children.text: sā ceyaṃ rītistridhā [bhidyate] / vaidarbhī , gauḍīyā , pāñcālī ceti //9//
children.translated_text: This <s>rīti</s> is of three kinds: <s>Vaidarbhī</s>, <s>Gauḍīyā</s>, and <s>Pāñcālī</s>. //9//

children.text: kiṃ punardeśavaśād dravyaguṇotpattiḥ kāvyānāṃ , yenā'yaṃ deśaviśeṣavyapadeśaḥ / naivaṃ , yadāha ----
children.translated_text: Is the production of qualities and materials in poetry determined by region, that there is this designation by specific regions? No, as he says —
The naming [of styles] is because they were observed in <s>Vidarbha</s> and other regions. // VKal_1,2.10 //

children.text: vidarbhagauḍapāñcāleṣu tatratyaiḥ kavibhiryathāsvarūpamupalabdhatvāt tatsamākhyā / na punardeśaiḥ kiñcidupakriyate kāvyānām //10//
children.translated_text: They are named thus because they were perceived in their respective forms by the poets of <s>Vidarbha</s>, <s>Gauḍa</s>, and <s>Pāñcāla</s>. But the regions do not contribute anything to the poetry. //10//
He states the distinction among these based on the difference of qualities —
<s>Vaidarbhī</s> is endowed with all the qualities. // VKal_1,2.11 //

children.text:
samagrairojaḥprasādapramukairguṇairupetā vaidarbhī nāma rītiḥ /
atra ślokaḥ ----
children.translated_text:
The style called <s>Vaidarbhī</s> is endowed with all the qualities, chief among which are <s>ojas</s> (vigor) and <s>prasāda</s> (clarity).
Here is a verse —
Untouched by any faults, strung together with all qualities,
endowed with the melodious beauty of a <s>vīṇā</s> — such is the <s>Vaidarbhī rīti</s> (style).
Poets thus praise it —
When the speaker is true, the meaning true, and the grammar correct,

children.text: asti tanna vinā yena parisravati vāṅmudhe //
children.translated_text: is there not something without which speech flows in vain?
Here is
an example (from <s>Śākuntala</s> 2.6) —

children.text:
gāhantāṃ mahiṣā nipānasalilaṃ śṛṅgairmuhustāḍitaṃ
  chāyāvaddhakadambakaṃ mṛgakulaṃ romanthamabhyasyatu //
children.translated_text:
Let the buffaloes plunge into the watering-pool, striking it repeatedly with their horns;
let the herds of deer, in clusters resting in the shade, chew the cud;

children.text:
visrabdhaṃ kurutāṃ varāhavitatirmustākṣatiṃ palvale
  viśrāntiṃ labhatāmidaṃ ca śithilajyābandhamasmaddhanuḥ //
children.translated_text:
let the throng of boars freely dig up <s>mustā</s> (nut-grass) roots in the marsh;
and let this bow of ours, its string-band loosened, find repose.
<s>Gauḍīyā</s> possesses <s>ojas</s> (vigor) and <s>kānti</s> (charm). // VKal_1,2.12 //

children.text: ojaḥ kānti.śca vidyete yasyāṃ sā ojaḥkāntimatī gauḍīyā nāma rītiḥ / mādhuryasaukumāryayorabhāvāt samāsabahulā atyulbaṇapadā ca / atra ślokaḥ ----
children.translated_text: That which has <s>ojas</s> (vigor) and <s>kānti</s> (charm) is the style called <s>Gauḍīyā</s> — abounding in compounds and with very prominent words, due to the absence of <s>mādhurya</s> (sweetness) and <s>saukumārya</s> (delicacy). Here is a verse —
With compound words and very prominent phrases, endowed with the qualities of <s>ojas</s> (vigor) and <s>kānti</s> (charm),
those versed in <s>rīti</s> (style) celebrate the <s>Gauḍīyā</s> style.
An example (from <s>Mahāvīracarita</s> 1.54) —
<s>Pāñcālī</s> is endowed with <s>mādhurya</s> (sweetness) and <s>saukumārya</s> (delicacy). // VKal_1,2.13 //

children.text: mādhruyeṇa saukumāryeṇa ca guṇonopapannā pāñcālī nāma rītiḥ / ojaḥkāntyabhāvādanulbaṇapadā vicchāyā ca / tathā ca ślokaḥ ----

children.translated_text: Of a mingled loose and tight character, endowed with the tinge of the ancient,

children.text: madhurāṃ sukumārāṃ ca pāñcālīṃ kavayo viduḥ //
children.translated_text: sweet and delicate — poets know this as the <s>Pāñcālī</s> [style].

The style called <s>Pāñcālī</s> is endowed with the qualities of sweetness and delicacy — with unobtrusive words and a dim lustre, due to the absence of <s>ojas</s> and <s>kānti</s>. And so the verse says —
As follows [example] —

children.text:
grāme 'sminpathikāya pāntha ! vasatirnaivādhunā dīyate
  rātrāvatra vihāramaṇḍapatale pānthaḥ prasupto yuvā /
  tenotthāya khalena gajati ghane smṛtvā priyāṃ tatkṛtaṃ
  yenādyāpi karaṅkadaṇḍapatanāśaṅkī janastiṣṭhati //
etāsu tisṛṣu rītiṣu rekhākhiva citraṃ kāvyaṃ pratiṣṭhatamiti //13//
children.translated_text: In these three styles, poetry stands firm, like a painting upon lines. //13//
Of these, the first is to be preferred, because of the completeness of qualities. // VKal_1,2.14 //

children.text: tāsāṃ tisṛṇāṃ rītīnāṃ pūrvā vaidarbhī grāhyā , guṇānāṃ sākalyāt //14//
children.translated_text: Of these three <s>rītis</s> (styles), the first, <s>Vaidarbhī</s>, is to be preferred, because of the completeness of its qualities. //14//
But not the others, because of their scarcity of qualities. // VKal_1,2.15 //
The others, <s>Gauḍīyā</s> and <s>Pāñcālī</s>, are not to be preferred, because of their scarcity of qualities. //15//
Some say that practice in the others is for the purpose of ascending to that [<s>Vaidarbhī</s>]. // VKal_1,2.16 //

children.text: tasyā vaidarbhyā evārohaṇārthamitarayorapi rītyorabhyāsa ityeke manyante //16//
children.translated_text: Some think that practice in the other two styles is for the purpose of ascending to that <s>Vaidarbhī</s> itself. //16//
But that is not so, because the truth does not arise from practicing what is not truth. // VKal_1,2.17 //
For the truth does not come about for one who practices the non-truth. //17//
He gives an illustration —
One who practices weaving hemp-thread cloth does not gain the varied beauty of silk-thread cloth. // VKal_1,2.18 //
A weaver who practices weaving hemp-thread cloth does not gain the varied beauty of silk-thread cloth. //18//
That [<s>Vaidarbhī</s>], when free of compound words, is pure <s>Vaidarbhī</s>. // VKal_1,2.19 //

children.text: sāpi vaidarbhī rītiḥ śuddhavaidarbhī bhaṇyate , yadi samāsavatpadaṃ na bhavati / /19//
children.translated_text: That <s>Vaidarbhī rīti</s> is called pure <s>Vaidarbhī</s> when there are no compound-heavy words. //19//
In it, the excellence of <s>artha-guṇas</s> (sense-qualities) is to be savored. // VKal_1,2.20 //
In that <s>Vaidarbhī</s>, the excellence of sense-qualities is to be savored. //20//
Through its foundation, even a trace of sense-quality [is effective]. // VKal_1,2.21 //

children.text: tadupadhānataḥ khalvarthaguṇaleśo'pi svadate / kimaṅga ! punararthaguṇasaṃpat / tathā cāhuḥ ----
children.translated_text: From its foundation, even a trace of sense-quality becomes delightful. How much more so the full excellence of sense-qualities! And thus they say —

children.text:
kiṃ tvasti kācidaparaiva padānupūrvī
  yasyāṃ na kiñcidapi kiñcidivāvabhāti /
children.translated_text: Is there then some other arrangement of words

children.text:
ānandayatytha ca karṇapathaṃ prayātā
  cetaḥ satāmamṛtavṛṣṭiriva praviṣṭā //
children.translated_text:
in which nothing at all appears as anything, yet
it delights and, having entered the path of the ear, enters the hearts of the good like a shower of nectar?

children.text:
vacasi yamadhiśayya syandate vācakaśrī-
  rvitathamavitathatvaṃ yatra vastu prayāti /
  udayati hi sa tādṛk kvāpi vaidarbharītau
  sahṛdayahṛdayānāṃ rañjakaḥ ko'pi pākaḥ //
children.translated_text:
Where the eloquence of expression flows resting upon the word,
where a thing truly goes beyond untruth —
there arises in the <s>Vaidarbhī rīti</s>, somewhere, that certain indefinable
ripeness that delights the hearts of the sensitive.
That [excellence of sense-qualities] too is [called] <s>Vaidarbhī</s>, through association. // VKal_1,2.22 //
This excellence of sense-qualities too is called <s>Vaidarbhī</s>. He shows by 'through association' that this is a figurative usage. //22//

children.text:
iti śrīpaṇḍitavaravāmanaviracitakāvyālaṅkārasūtravṛttau śārīre prathame 'dhikaraṇe dvitīyo'dhyāyaḥ /
adhikāricintā , rītiniścayaśca /
children.translated_text:
Thus ends the second chapter of the first section on the body in the commentary on the <s>Kāvyālaṅkāra-sūtras</s> composed by the eminent scholar <s>Vāmana</s>.
Investigation of the qualified student, and determination of <s>rīti</s> (style).
Now, the third chapter of the first section.
Having determined the investigation of the qualified student and the reality of <s>rīti</s>, he says, in order to show the constituents of poetry —

children.text: loko vidyā prakīrṇa ca kāvyāṅgāni // VKal_1,3.1 //
children.translated_text: World-knowledge, learning, and miscellaneous matters are the constituents of poetry. // VKal_1,3.1 //
He explains this in the order of enumeration —
The world is the ways of worldly life. // VKal_1,3.2 //
The world — consisting of the animate and inanimate — its behavior is its ways. //2//
Grammar, tradition, lexicon, prosody, arts, erotic science, political science — these preceded [as] the branches of learning. // VKal_1,3.3 //
The precedence of grammar, tradition, and the rest means that they are to be attended to first in the composition of poetry. //3//
In order to explain their role as constituents of poetry, he says —
From grammar comes the purity of words. // VKal_1,3.4 //

children.text: śabdasmṛtervyākaraṇācchabdānāṃ śuddhiḥ sādhutvaniścayaḥ kartavyaḥ / śuddhāni hi padāni niḥśaṅkaiḥ kavibhiḥ prayujyante //4//
children.translated_text: From grammar — the science of words — the purity of words, the determination of correctness, is to be effected. For pure words are used without hesitation by poets. //4//
From the lexicon comes the determination of word-meanings. // VKal_1,3.5 //

children.text: padaṃ hi racanāprapraveśayogyaṃ bhāvayan saṃdigdhārthatvena na gṛhṇīyānna vā jahyāditi kāvyabandhavighnaḥ / tasmādabhidhānakośataḥ padārthaniścayaḥ kartavya iti / apūrvābhidhānalābhārthatvaṃ tvayuktamabhidhānakośasya , aprayuktasyāprayojyatvāt / yadi prayuktaṃ prayujyate tarhi kimiti saṃdighāthatvamāśaṅkitaṃ padasya ? tanna ; tatra sāmānyenārthāvagatiḥ saṃbhavati / yathā {nīvī}śabdena jaghanavasragranthirucyata iti kasyacinnaścayaḥ / striyā vā puruṣasya veti saṃśayaḥ

children.translated_text: <s>Nīvī</s> is the knotting of a woman's garment at the waist —
thus one sees the entry in the name-lexicon. Now how [does this apply]? —

A word that is fit to enter into composition, if not understood or rejected because its meaning is doubtful, becomes an obstacle to poetic composition. Therefore, the determination of word-meanings from the lexicon is necessary. But the purpose of the lexicon is not for acquiring new words, for what is not in use should not be used. If what is in use is being used, then why is doubt about the word's meaning feared? That is not so; there, only a general understanding of the meaning is possible. For example, someone has the certainty that the word <s>nīvī</s> means 'the knot of a garment at the waist'; but the doubt is: of a woman or of a man?
With expanding ribs, growing from the enjoyment of various foods,
the waist-knot, though tied by someone before, was loosened.
Such is the usage. [It may work] through error or figurative application. //5//
From the science of prosody comes the resolution of doubt about meters. // VKal_1,3.6 //

children.text: kāvyābhyāsādvṛttasaṃkrāntirbhavatyeva / kiṃ tu mātrāvṛttādiṣu kvacitsaṃśayaḥ syāt / ato vṛttasaṃśayacchedaśchandovicitervidheya iti //6//
children.translated_text: From the practice of poetry, the transfer of meters certainly occurs. However, in syllabic meters and the like, doubt may sometimes arise. Therefore, the resolution of doubt about meters is to be effected from the science of prosody. //6//
From the treatises on arts comes the knowledge of the reality of arts. // VKal_1,3.7 //

children.text: kalā gītanṛtyacitrādikāstāsāmabhidhāyakāni śāstrāṇi viśākhilādipraṇītāni kalāśāstrāṇi , tebhyaḥ kalātattvasya saṃvit saṃvedanam / na hi kalātattvānupalabdhau kalāvastu samyaṅnibandhuṃ śakyamiti //7//
children.translated_text: The <s>kalās</s> (arts) are music, dance, painting, and so on; the <s>śāstras</s> (treatises) that expound them, composed by <s>Viśākhila</s> and others, are the <s>kalā-śāstras</s> (treatises on the arts). From these comes the knowledge — the understanding — of the essence of the arts. For without comprehending the essence of the arts, it is impossible to compose well on artistic subjects. //7//
From the <s>Kāmaśāstra</s> (treatise on love), [knowledge] of the practice of love. // VKal_1,3.8 //
'Knowledge'

children.text: ityanuvartate / kāmopacārasya saṃvit kāmaśāstrata iti / kāmopacārabahulaṃ hi vastu kāvyasyeti //8//
children.translated_text: is carried forward [from the previous sūtra]. The knowledge of the practice of love comes from the <s>Kāmaśāstra</s>. For the subject matter of poetry is abundantly concerned with love. //8//
From the <s>Daṇḍanīti</s> (science of governance), [knowledge] of policy and malpolicy. // VKal_1,3.9 //

children.text: daṇḍanīterarthaśāstrānnayasyāpanayasya ca saṃviditi / tatra ṣāḍguṇyasya yathāvatorayogo nayaḥ / tadviparīto'panayaḥ / na hi tāvavijñāya nāyakapratināyakayorvṛttaṃ śakyaṃ kāvye nibandhumiti //9//
children.translated_text: From the <s>Daṇḍanīti</s>, i.e. <s>Arthaśāstra</s> (political science), [comes] the knowledge of <s>naya</s> (wise policy) and <s>apanaya</s> (unwise policy). Here, <s>naya</s> is the proper application of the sixfold strategy (<s>ṣāḍguṇya</s>). <s>Apanaya</s> is its opposite. For without knowing these, one cannot compose in poetry the conduct of the protagonist and antagonist. //9//
And from that [comes] the complexity of the plot. // VKal_1,3.10 //

children.text: itihāsādiritivṛttaṃ kāvyaśarīram , tasya kuṭilatvaṃ tato daṇḍanīterbalīvastvābalīyastvādiprayogo vyutpattimūlatvāttasyāḥ / evamanyāsāmapi vidyānāṃ yathāsvamupayogo varṇanīya iti //10//
children.translated_text: The <s>itivṛtta</s> (plot), derived from history and the like, is the body of poetry. Its <s>kuṭilatva</s> (complexity) comes from the <s>Daṇḍanīti</s> — the employment of tactics such as overpowering the strong and empowering the weak — because that [science] is the root of expertise. Similarly, the respective utility of other branches of knowledge should also be described. //10//

children.text: lakṣyajñatvamabhiyogo vṛddhasevāvekṣaṇaṃ pratibhānamavadhānaṃ ca prakīrṇam // VKal_1,3.11 //
children.translated_text: Familiarity with exemplary works, practice, service of elders, critical examination, creative inspiration, and concentration — these are miscellaneous [requisites]. // VKal_1,3.11 //
Of these, familiarity with poetry constitutes knowledge of exemplary works. // VKal_1,3.12 //

children.text: anyeṣāṃ kāvyeṣu paricayo lakṣyajñatvam / tato hi kāvyabandhasya vyutpattirbhavati //12//
children.translated_text: Familiarity with the poems of others constitutes <s>lakṣyajñatva</s> (knowledge of exemplary works). From that indeed arises expertise in poetic composition. //12//
Effort in poetic composition is <s>abhiyoga</s> (practice). // VKal_1,3.13 //

children.text: bandhanaṃ bandhaḥ , kāvyasya bandho racanā kāvyabandhaḥ / tatrodyamo'bhiyogaḥ / sa hi kavitvaprakarṣamādadhāti //13//
children.translated_text: <s>Bandhana</s> is <s>bandha</s> (composition); the <s>bandha</s> (composition) of poetry, i.e., its construction, is <s>kāvyabandha</s>. Effort therein is <s>abhiyoga</s> (practice). For that indeed brings about excellence in poetic skill. //13//
Devoted service to teachers of poetic instruction is <s>vṛddhasevā</s> (service of elders). // VKal_1,3.14 //

children.text: kāvyopadeśe gurava upadeṣṭāraḥ / teṣāṃ śuśrūṣaṇaṃ vṛddhasevā / tataḥ kāvyavidyāyāḥ saṃkrāntirbhavati //14//
children.translated_text: The <s>gurus</s> (teachers) are the instructors in poetry. Devoted service to them is <s>vṛddhasevā</s> (service of elders). From that comes the transmission of the science of poetry. //14//
The placing and removing of words is <s>avekṣaṇa</s> (critical examination). // VKal_1,3.15 //

children.text: padasyādhānaṃ nyāsaḥ , uddharaṇamapasāraṇam / tayoḥ khalvavekṣaṇam / atra ślokau ----
children.translated_text: The <s>ādhāna</s> (placing) of a word is its setting down; <s>uddharaṇa</s> (removing) is its taking away. The examination of these two indeed [constitutes avekṣaṇa]. Here are two verses —
The placing and removing [of words continues] as long as the mind

children.text: padasya sthāpite sthairye hanta siddhā sarasvatī //
children.translated_text: vacillates; when stability in the word is established — behold, <s>Sarasvatī</s> (eloquence) is attained!

children.text:
yatpadāni tyajantyeva parivṛttisahiṣṇutām /
  taṃ śabdanyāsaniṣṇātāḥ śabdapākaṃ pracakṣate //
children.translated_text:
That [quality] by which words abandon tolerance for substitution —
those skilled in the placement of words call that <s>śabdapāka</s> (maturity of expression).
The seed of poetic genius is <s>pratibhāna</s> (creative inspiration). // VKal_1,3.16 //

children.text: kavitvasya bījaṃ kavitvabījaṃ janmāntarāgatasaṃskāraviśeṣaḥ kaścit , yasmādvinā kāvyaṃ na niṣpadyate , niṣpannaṃ vāvahāsāyatanaṃ syāt //16// ++
children.translated_text: The seed of poetic genius is <s>kavitvabīja</s> — a certain special <s>saṃskāra</s> (mental impression) acquired from a previous birth, without which poetry is not produced, or if produced, would be an object of ridicule. //16//
One-pointedness of mind is <s>avadhāna</s> (concentration). // VKal_1,3.17 //

children.text: cittasyaikāgryaṃ bāhyārthanivṛttiḥ tadavadhānam / avahitaṃ hi cittamarthān paśyati //17//
children.translated_text: The one-pointedness of the mind, i.e., withdrawal from external objects, is <s>avadhāna</s> (concentration). For an attentive mind perceives the meanings [of things]. //17//
That [concentration arises] from place and time. // VKal_1,3.18 //
That <s>avadhāna</s> (concentration) arises from place and time. //18//
What then are the [proper] place and time? To this he says —
A secluded place. // VKal_1,3.19 //
A secluded, solitary [place]. //19//
The fourth watch of the night is the [proper] time. // VKal_1,3.20 //

children.text: rātreryāmo rātriyāmaḥ praharaḥ turīyaścaturthaḥ kāla iti / tadvaśādviṣayoparataṃ cittaṃ prasannamavadhatte //20//
children.translated_text: A <s>yāma</s> (watch) of the night is a <s>rātriyāma</s>, i.e. a <s>prahara</s> (three-hour period). The fourth one is the [proper] time. Under its influence, the mind, withdrawn from sense objects, becomes clear and attentive. //20//
Having thus set forth the constituents of poetry, he speaks for the purpose of understanding the particular types of poetry —
Poetry is of two kinds: <s>gadya</s> (prose) and <s>padya</s> (verse). // VKal_1,3.21 //

children.text: gadyasya pūrvaṃ nirdeśo durlakṣyaviṣayatvena durbandhatvāt / yathāhuḥ ----

children.translated_text: "Prose is the touchstone of poets."
Prose is mentioned first because its subject matter is harder to discern and its composition more difficult. As they say —
To show that it is divided into three kinds, he says —
Prose is <s>vṛttagandhi</s> (having a trace of metre), <s>cūrṇa</s> (flowing), and <s>utkalikāprāya</s> (predominantly compounded). // VKal_1,3.22 //
He states their definitions —
<s>Vṛttagandhi</s> is that which contains portions of verse. // VKal_1,3.23 //
"Among the <s>Dānavas</s> dwelling in the depths of the netherworld"
and so on.

children.text: atra hi vasantatilakākhyasya vṛttasya bhāgaḥ pratyabhijñāyate //23//
children.translated_text: For here a portion of the metre called <s>Vasantatilaka</s> is recognizable. //23//

The portions (<s>bhāgas</s>) of verse are <s>padyabhāgas</s>; prose having those is <s>vṛttagandhi</s>.
For example:
<s>Cūrṇa</s> (flowing prose) is that with graceful, uncompounded words. // VKal_1,3.24 //

children.text: anāviddhānyadīrghasamāsāni lalitānyanuddhatāni padāni yasmiṃstadanāviddhalalitapadaṃ cūrṇamiti / yathā ----
children.translated_text: <s>Anāviddha</s> means free from excessively long compounds; <s>lalita</s> means gentle, not bombastic — prose whose words are such is called <s>anāviddha-lalita-pada</s>, i.e. <s>cūrṇa</s> (flowing prose). For example —

children.text:
abhyāso hi karmaṇāṃ kauśalamāvahati /
  na hi sakṛnnipātamātreṇodabindurapi grāvaṇi nimnatāmādadhāti /
children.translated_text:
"Practice indeed brings skill in actions.
For a drop of water does not create a depression in a stone by a single fall alone."
The opposite is <s>utkalikāprāya</s> (predominantly compounded). // VKal_1,3.25 //
The opposite — having piercing, elevated words — is <s>utkalikāprāya</s>. For example —

"Upon the lion, whose face is radiant with the beautiful mass of mane drenched by the streams of rut flowing from the temple-surfaces of mighty elephants split open by the fierce blows of its thunderbolt-peak-hard claws"
and so on. //25//
Verse is of many kinds. // VKal_1,3.26 //

children.text: padyaṃ khalvanekena samārdhasamaviṣamādinā bhedena bhinnaṃ bhavati //26//
children.translated_text: Verse indeed is divided into many varieties such as <s>sama</s> (even), <s>ardhasama</s> (half-even), <s>viṣama</s> (uneven), and so forth. //26//
That [poetry] is <s>anibaddha</s> (unbound) and <s>nibaddha</s> (bound). // VKal_1,3.27 //

children.text: tadidaṃ gadyapadyarūpaṃ kāvyamanibaddhaṃ nibaddhaṃ ca / anayoḥ prasiddhatvāllakṣaṇaṃ noktam //27//
children.translated_text: This poetry, in the form of prose and verse, is <s>anibaddha</s> (a collection of independent verses) and <s>nibaddha</s> (a connected composition). Since both are well-known, their definitions are not given. //27//
Their sequential attainment is like that of a garland and a crest-jewel. // VKal_1,3.28 //

children.text: tayorityanibaddhaṃ nibaddhaṃ ca parāmṛśyate / krameṇa siddhiḥ kramasiddhiḥ / anibaddhasiddhau nibaddhasiddhaiḥ sraguttaṃsavat / yathā sraji mālāyā siddhāyāmuttaṃsaḥ śekharaḥ sidhyati //28//
children.translated_text: 'Of the two' refers to <s>anibaddha</s> and <s>nibaddha</s>. Sequential attainment means achievement in order. After success in <s>anibaddha</s> comes success in <s>nibaddha</s>, like a garland and its crest-jewel — just as when the garland is accomplished, the crest-jewel is achieved. //28//
Some have been content with <s>anibaddha</s> alone; to criticize that, he says —
<s>Anibaddha</s> does not shine, like a single luminous atom. // VKal_1,3.29 //

children.text:
na khalvanibaddhaṃ kāvyaṃ cakāsti dīpyate / yathaikatejaḥparamāṇuriti /
atra ślokaḥ ----
children.translated_text:
<s>Anibaddha</s> poetry does not shine, does not radiate brilliance — just like a single luminous atom.
Here is a verse —
Poems that are not composed into a whole have no beauty;
luminous atoms do not shine individually.
Among connected compositions, the <s>daśarūpaka</s> (ten dramatic forms) is the best. // VKal_1,3.30 //
Among <s>saṃdarbhas</s> (connected compositions), the <s>daśarūpaka</s>, beginning with <s>nāṭaka</s> (drama), is the best. //30//
Why? To this he says —
For it is variegated like a painted canvas, due to the completeness of its special features. // VKal_1,3.31 //

children.text: taddaśarūpakaṃ hi yasmāñcitraṃ citrapaṭacat / viśeṣāṇāṃ sākalyāt //31//
children.translated_text: That <s>daśarūpaka</s> indeed is variegated like a painted canvas, because of the completeness of its special features. //31//
From that, the classification of other types is derived. // VKal_1,3.32 //

children.text: tato daśarūpakādanyeṣāṃ bhedānāṃ kḷptiḥ kalpanamiti / daśarūpakasyaiva hīdaṃ sarvaṃ vilasitam , yacca kathākhyāyike mahākāvyamiti / tallakṣaṇaṃ ca nātīva hṛdayaṅgamamityupekṣitamasmābhiḥ / tadanyato grāhyam //32//
children.translated_text: From the <s>daśarūpaka</s>, the classification of other forms is derived, i.e. devised. For all this — whether <s>kathā</s> (tale), <s>ākhyāyikā</s> (narrative), or <s>mahākāvya</s> (epic poem) — is but a manifestation of the <s>daśarūpaka</s> alone. Their definitions, being not very compelling, have been passed over by us. They should be learned from other sources. //32//
Thus ends the third chapter of the first section, the <s>Śārīra</s> (body), in the <s>Kāvyālaṅkārasūtravṛtti</s> of <s>Śrī Vāmana</s>. //1-3//
Thus concludes the first section, the <s>Śārīra</s> (body).
First chapter of the second section.

children.text: kāvyaśarīre sthāpite kāvyasaundaryākṣepahetavastyāgāya doṣā vijñātavyā iti doṣadarśanaṃ nāmādhikaraṇamārabhyate / doṣasvarūpakathārthamāha ----
children.translated_text: Having established the body of poetry, the section on <s>doṣa-darśana</s> (perception of defects) is begun, for the purpose of rejecting the causes that would diminish poetic beauty, [since] defects must be understood. To state the nature of defects, he says —
Defects are the opposites of <s>guṇas</s> (excellences). // VKal_2,1.1 //
The opposites of the <s>guṇas</s> (excellences) to be described — those constitute the nature of defects. //1//
Their understanding follows from the meaning [of the guṇas]. // VKal_2,1.2 //
From the determination of the nature of the <s>guṇas</s>, the understanding of those defects follows implicitly, i.e. is established. //2//
Why then are they elaborated separately? To this he says —
The elaboration is for the sake of ease [of understanding]. // VKal_2,1.3 //

children.text: saukaryārthaḥ prapañco vistaro doṣānām / uddiṣṭā lakṣaṇalakṣitā hi doṣāḥ sujñānā bhavanti //3//
children.translated_text: The elaboration, i.e. detailed exposition, of defects is for the sake of ease. For defects that have been enumerated and defined by their characteristics are easily recognized. //3//
To show the defects of words, he says —

children.text: duṣṭaṃ padamasādhu kaṣṭaṃ grāmyamapratītamanarthakaṃ ca // VKal_2,1.4 //
children.translated_text: A faulty word is one that is ungrammatical, harsh-sounding, vulgar, unfamiliar, or meaningless. // VKal_2,1.4 //
To explain [these] in order, he says —
That which is contrary to grammar is ungrammatical (<s>asādhu</s>). // VKal_2,1.5 //
"The purposelessness of another case-ending"
Here indeed,
according to the rule regarding the sixth case, the third case, and others,
the form <s>duk</s> should have been used. //5//
A word that is contrary to <s>śabdasmṛti</s>, i.e. grammar, is ungrammatical. For example —
That which is harsh to the ear is <s>kaṣṭa</s> (harsh-sounding). // VKal_2,1.6 //

children.text: śrutivirasaṃ śrotrakaṭu padaṃ kaṣṭam / taddhi racanāgumphitamapyudvejayati / yathā ----

children.translated_text: "O fierce one! The moon quickly steals from your cheeks the fluid of beauty!"
A word that is harsh to the ear, grating to the hearing, is <s>kaṣṭa</s> (harsh-sounding). For even when woven into a composition, it causes displeasure. For example —
That which is used only in common speech is <s>grāmya</s> (vulgar). // VKal_2,1.7 //

children.text: loka eva yasprayuktaṃ padaṃ , na śāstre ; tadgrāmyam / yathā

children.translated_text: "Alas, how she weeps, puffing!"
Other [words] such as <s>lagalla</s> and the like should also be noted. //7//
A word that is used only in common speech, not in learned treatises, is <s>grāmya</s> (vulgar). For example:
That which is used only in technical treatises is <s>apratīta</s> (unfamiliar). // VKal_2,1.8 //

children.text: śāstra eva prayuktaṃ yat , na loke tadapratītaṃ padam / yathā ----
children.translated_text: A word that is used only in learned treatises, not in common speech, is <s>apratīta</s> (unfamiliar). For example —

children.text: kiṃ bhāṣitena bahunā rūpaskandhasya santi me na guṇāḥ /
children.translated_text: "What use is much speech? Do I not possess the qualities of <s>rūpaskandha</s> (form-aggregate)?
And <s>āntarīyaka</s> (undergarment) is a standard of measurement — so you have no ground for reproach."
Here the words <s>rūpaskandha</s> and <s>āntarīyaka</s> are not [used] in common speech, hence they are unfamiliar. //8//
That which serves merely as a filler is <s>anarthaka</s> (meaningless). // VKal_2,1.9 //

An indeclinable word whose sole purpose is to fill [the metre] is <s>anarthaka</s> (meaningless). By the principle of <s>daṇḍāpūpa</s> (stick and cake), another word too is similarly meaningless. For example —

children.text: uditastu hāstikavinīlamayaṃ timiraṃ nipīya kiraṇaiḥ savitā /
children.translated_text: "Having drunk the darkness, blue as an elephant, with its rays, the sun has risen."

children.text:
atra {tu}śabdasya pādapūraṇārthameva prayogaḥ /
  na vākyālaṅkārārtham [k: // *VKal_2,1.10//]
vākyālaṅkāraprayojanaṃ tu nānarthakam / apavādārthamidam /
[k: apavādārthamidam / vākyālaṅkāraprayojanaṃ tu nānarthakam /]
yathā ----
children.translated_text:
Here the word <s>tu</s> is used merely for filling the metrical foot.
But when serving as a poetic ornament, it is not meaningless. This is stated as an exception.
For example —

children.text: na khalviha gatāgatā nayanagocaraṃ me gatā
children.translated_text: "Indeed, she who went and came has not gone from the range of my eyes"
and so on.
Similarly <s>hi</s>, <s>khalu</s>, <s>hanta</s>, and the like. //9//
Now he states the defects of word-meaning —
<s>Anyārtha</s> (wrongly directed), <s>neyagūḍhārtha</s> (obscure in meaning), <s>aślīla</s> (indecent), and <s>kliṣṭa</s> (forced) — these too [are defective]. // VKal_2,1.10 //
'A faulty word'

children.text: ityanuvartate / arthataśca vacanavipariṇāmaḥ / anyārthādīni padāni duṣṭānīti sūtrārthaḥ //10//
children.translated_text: is carried forward [from above]. And from the standpoint of meaning, there is a modification of the statement. Words such as <s>anyārtha</s> and others are defective — this is the meaning of the <s>sūtra</s>. //10//
To define these in order, he says —
<s>Anyārtha</s> (wrongly directed) is that which deviates from established usage. // VKal_2,1.11 //

children.text: rūḍhicyutam, rūḍhimanapekṣya yaugikārthamātropādānāt / anyārthaṃ padam / sthūlatvātsāmānyena ghaṭaśabdaḥ paṭaśabdātha ityādikamanyārthaṃ noktam / yathā ----
children.translated_text: That which deviates from established usage (<s>rūḍhi</s>), i.e. employs only the etymological meaning without regard for conventional meaning, is <s>anyārtha</s>. Due to the grossness [of the error], common instances such as using the word <s>ghaṭa</s> (pot) for <s>paṭa</s> (cloth) are not mentioned. For example —
"They bring suffering, both great and small, those who remember beloved unions."

children.text: atra-āvahatiḥ karotyartho dhāraṇārthe prayuktaḥ , prasmaratirvismaraṇārthaḥ prakṛṣṭasmaraṇe iti //11//
children.translated_text: Here <s>āvahati</s> (to bring), which means 'to do,' is used in the sense of 'to bear,' and <s>prasmarati</s> (to forget) is used in the sense of 'to remember intensely.' //11//
That whose meaning is contrived is <s>neyārtha</s> (requiring interpretation). // VKal_2,1.12 //
<s>Neyārtha</s> is that in which the meaning of the word, though not directly heard, must be inferred and contrived. For example —
"The army of monkeys, arranged in rows like a flock of birds, accompanied by the strong son of the bearer [of mountains],
was conquered by the one who defeated the owls, with sharp arrows raining like a great mountain."

children.text: atra vihaṅgamaścakravāko 'bhipretaḥ / tannāmāni cakrāṇi , tāni bibhratīti vihaṅgamanāmabhṛto rathāḥ / paṅktiriti daśasaṃkhyā lakṣyate / paṅktirdaśa vihaṅgamanāmabhṛto rathā yasya sa paṅktivihaṅgamanāmabhṛddaśarathaḥ / tasya tanayābhyāṃ rāmalakṣmaṇābhyāṃ saṃvalitaṃ plavagasainyaṃ jitam / ulūkajitā indrajitā / {kauśika}śabdendrplūkayorabhidhānamiti {kauśika}śabdavācyatvenendra ulūka uktaḥ / nanu caivaṃ rathāṅganāmādīnāmapi prayogo'nupapannaḥ , ---- na ; teṣāṃ nirūḍhalakṣaṇatvāt //12//
children.translated_text: Here, the bird referred to is the <s>cakravāka</s>. The wheels (<s>cakra</s>) are its name, and 'bearing the names of birds' means chariots bearing those names. '<s>Paṅkti</s>' indicates the number ten. '<s>Paṅkti</s>' [means] ten; 'bearing the names of birds as chariots' — one who has ten such chariots is <s>Paṅkti-vihaṅgama-nāmabhṛd-daśa-ratha</s> (i.e., <s>Daśaratha</s>). By the two sons of that [king], <s>Rāma</s> and <s>Lakṣmaṇa</s>, accompanied by the monkey army, he was defeated. '<s>Ulūka-jita</s>' means 'conquered by the owl' (i.e., <s>Indrajit</s>). Since the word '<s>kauśika</s>' denotes both <s>Indra</s> and an owl, <s>Indra</s> is indicated as an owl through the word '<s>kauśika</s>.' Now, if this is so, the use of words like '<s>rathāṅga-nāma</s>' and others would also be unjustified — no, because those have well-established secondary meanings. //12//
That which employs a word in an unfamiliar sense is called <s>gūḍhārtha</s> (obscure meaning). // VKal_2,1.13 //

children.text: yasya padasya loke'rthaḥ prasiddhaśrāprāseddhaśca , tadprasiddhe'rthe prayuktaṃ gūḍhārtham / yathā ----
children.translated_text: A word whose meaning is well-known in common usage and not well-known [in a different sense] — when used in that unfamiliar sense, it is <s>gūḍhārtha</s>. For example —
'An army like [that of] <s>Sahasragu</s> (<s>Indra</s>), unbearable by many enemies.'
Thus.

children.text: sahasraṃ gāvo 'kṣīṇi yasya sa sahasragurindraḥ / tasyeveti gośabdasyākṣivācitvaṃ kaviṣvaprasiddhamiti //13//
children.translated_text: <s>Sahasragu</s> — one who has a thousand 'cows' (i.e., eyes) — is <s>Indra</s>. Thus, the word '<s>go</s>' meaning 'eye' is unfamiliar among poets. //13//
That which has an indecent alternative meaning or causes the recollection of indecency is called <s>aślīla</s> (vulgar). // VKal_2,1.14 //
'<s>Varcas</s>'

children.text:
iti padaṃ tejasi viṣṭhāyāṃ ca /
yattu padaṃ sabhyārthavācakamapyekadeśadvāreṇāsabhyārthaṃ smārayati , tadasabhyasmṛtihetuḥ / yathā ----
children.translated_text: — this word [means] both 'radiance' and 'excrement.' But a word that, though expressing a decent meaning, recalls something indecent through a partial resemblance — that is a cause of indecent recollection. For example —
'<s>Kṛkāṭikā</s>' (nape of the neck)
A word with multiple meanings, one of which is indecent — that has an indecent alternative meaning. For example —
The <s>gupta</s> (concealed), <s>lakṣita</s> (marked), and <s>saṃvṛta</s> (covered) [types] are not [considered vulgar]. // VKal_2,1.15 //

children.text: apavādārthamidam / guptaṃ lakṣitaṃ saṃvṛttaṃ ca nāślīlam //15//
children.translated_text: This is stated as an exception. The concealed, the marked, and the covered are not <s>aślīla</s> (vulgar). //15//
He states the definitions of these —
That whose indecent [meaning] is unfamiliar is <s>gupta</s> (concealed). // VKal_2,1.16 //
'<s>Saṃbādha</s>' (narrow/confined)

children.text: iti padam / taddhi saṃkaṭārthaṃ prasiddham , na guhyārthamiti //16//
children.translated_text: — this word. For it is well-known in the meaning of 'narrow passage,' not in the indecent meaning. //16//
A word whose indecent alternative meaning is unfamiliar — that is <s>gupta</s> (concealed). For example —
That which is connected with an indecent meaning through secondary signification is <s>lakṣita</s> (marked). // VKal_2,1.17 //
'<s>Janmabhū</s>' (birthplace)

children.text: iti / taddhi lakṣaṇayā guṇātham , na svaśaktyeti //17//
children.translated_text: — this word. For it conveys the meaning through secondary signification, not through its own primary power. //17//
When a word with an indecent alternative meaning is connected with an indecent sense through <s>lakṣaṇā</s> (secondary signification), it is <s>lakṣita</s>. For example —
That which is socially accepted is <s>saṃvṛta</s> (covered). // VKal_2,1.18 //

children.text: lokena saṃvītaṃ lokasaṃvītaṃ yat tat saṃvṛtam / yathā ----

children.translated_text: '<s>Subhagā</s>' (fortunate/beautiful woman)
'<s>Bhaga</s>' refers to the female organ; the intended meaning is 'the longing of a maiden.'
Here is the verse —
That which is accepted by the world — socially accepted — is <s>saṃvṛta</s> (covered). For example —

children.text: saṃvītasya hi lokena na doṣānveṣaṇaṃ ksamam /
children.translated_text: 'It is not proper to search for faults in that which is socially accepted;
who would think of indecency in the form of a <s>Śivaliṅga</s>?'
It is of three kinds, based on the divisions of causing shame, disgust, and inauspicious dread. // VKal_2,1.19 //

children.text: tasyāślīlasya traividhyaṃ bhavati , vrīḍājugupsāmaṅgalātaṅkadāyināṃ bhedāt / kiñcit vrīḍādāyi bhavati / yathā ----

children.translated_text: '<s>Vāk-kāṭava</s>' (garrulous), '<s>Hiraṇyaretas</s>' (one whose seed is gold [i.e., fire])
Thus. Some cause disgust. For example —
'<s>Kapardaka</s>' (a small coin / matted hair)
Thus. Some cause inauspicious dread. For example —
'<s>Saṃsthita</s>' (established / dead)
That <s>aślīla</s> (vulgarity) is threefold, based on the distinctions of causing shame, disgust, and inauspicious dread. Some cause shame. For example —
That in which the apprehension of meaning is obstructed is called <s>kliṣṭa</s> (labored). // VKal_2,1.20 //

children.text: arthasya pratītirarthapratyayaḥ / sa vyavahito yasmādbhavati tadvyavahitārthapratyayaṃ kliṣṭam / yathā ----
children.translated_text: The comprehension of meaning is <s>artha-pratyaya</s>; that from which it becomes obstructed — that is <s>vyavahitārthapratyaya</s>, [meaning] <s>kliṣṭa</s> (labored). For example —
'From the starry daughters of <s>Dakṣa</s>, the beloved of their lover [the Moon], drops of water fall tremblingly upon their moonstone platforms.'

children.text: dakṣātmajāstārāḥ / tāsāṃ dayito dakṣātmajādayitaścandraḥ / tasya vallabhāścandrakāntāḥ / tadvedikānāmiti / atra hi vyavadhānenārthapratyayaḥ //20//
children.translated_text: The daughters of <s>Dakṣa</s> are the stars. Their beloved is the Moon, the darling of <s>Dakṣa's</s> daughters. His beloveds are the moonstones. 'Upon their platforms' — here, the apprehension of meaning occurs through obstruction [i.e., through a convoluted compound]. //20//
Not [labored] if the meaning is readily grasped, even when not well-established. // VKal_2,1.21 //

children.text: arūḍhāvapi yato'rthapratyayo jhaṭiti na tatkliṣṭam / yathā ----
children.translated_text: Even if the meaning is not well-established, if it is grasped instantly, it is not <s>kliṣṭa</s> (labored). For example —
'The waist, the string of ornaments, and the region of the blameless one.'
Thus.
By the last two [faults], the sentence is also explained. // VKal_2,1.22 //

children.text:
aślīlaṃ kliṣṭaṃ cetyantye pade / tābhyāṃ vākyaṃ vyākhyātam / tadapyaślīlaṃ kliṣṭaṃ ca bhavati /
aślīlaṃ yathā ----
children.translated_text: <s>Aślīla</s> (vulgar) and <s>kliṣṭa</s> (labored) — these are the last two terms. By these, the sentence is also explained; it too can be vulgar and labored. Vulgar, for example —
'That prosperity is not one that bestows pleasure at one's leisure;
of those whose side-regions are bound for others' sake, the wealth that is true is [merely] soft.'

children.text:
sopānapathamutsṛjya vāyuvegasamuddhatam /
  mahāpathena gatavān kīrtyamānaguṇo janaiḥ //
children.translated_text: 'Abandoning the stairway, carried up by the force of the wind, he went by the great path, his virtues being celebrated by the people.'
Labored, for example —

children.text: dhammillasya na kasya prekṣya nikāmaṃ kuraṅgaśāvākṣyāḥ /
children.translated_text: 'Whose mind does not become enamored, seeing at leisure the beauty of the hairstyle
of the doe-eyed one, novel in its arrangement and composition?'
Having understood these faults of words and word-meanings, a poet should avoid them — this is the purport.

children.text: iti śrīkāvyālaṅkārasūtravṛttau doṣadarśane dvitīye'dhikaraṇe prathamo'dhyāyaḥ padapadārthadoṣavibhāgaḥ /
children.translated_text: Thus ends the first chapter on the classification of faults of words and word-meanings, in the second section on the examination of faults, in the <s>Kāvyālaṅkārasūtravṛtti</s>.
The second chapter in the second section.
Having explained the faults of words and word-meanings, he now proceeds to show the faults of sentences —
Sentences may have broken meter, faulty caesura, or bad conjunction. // VKal_2,2.1 //
This is a general statement of their connection [with faults]. //1//
He explains them in order —
That whose meter deviates from its own definition is called <s>bhinnavṛtta</s> (broken meter). // VKal_2,2.2 //

children.text: svasmāllakṣaṇāccyutaṃ vṛttaṃ yasmiṃstat svalakṣaṇacyutaṃ vākyaṃ bhinnavṛttam / yathā ----
children.translated_text: A sentence whose meter has deviated from its own defining characteristics is <s>bhinnavṛtta</s> (broken meter). For example —
'Ah, do you see the one who has ascended the palace, bearing an unbroken garland of flowers?'

children.text: vaitālīyayugmapāde laghvakṣarāṇāṃ paṇṇāṃ nairantaryaṃ nipiddham / tacca kṛtamiti bhinnavṛttatvam //2//
children.translated_text: In the second <s>pāda</s> of the <s>Vaitālīya</s> meter, the required sequence of light syllables is violated. And that is done [here] — hence, it is a case of broken meter. //2//
That which has a displeasing pause is called <s>yatibhraṣṭa</s> (faulty caesura). // VKal_2,2.3 //
That in which the pause is harsh to the ear — that is <s>yatibhraṣṭa</s> (faulty caesura). //3//
That [faulty caesura] occurs generally when there is a split in the verbal root portion or in the nominal portion, caused by vowel <s>sandhi</s>. // VKal_2,2.4 //

children.text: tad yatibhraṣṭaṃ dhātubhāgabhede nāmabhāgabhede ca sati bhavati / svarasandhinā kṛte prāyeṇa bāhulyena / dhātubhāgabhede mandākrāntāyāṃ yathā
children.translated_text: That faulty caesura occurs when there is a split in the verbal root portion or in the nominal portion, generally caused by vowel <s>sandhi</s>. In the case of a split in the verbal root portion, in the <s>Mandākrāntā</s> meter, for example —
'Of these flowers, a garland hanging from the neck shines forth.'
In the case of a split in the nominal portion, in the <s>Śikharīṇī</s> meter, for example —
'Perspiration spreads on the cheek-surfaces of the doe-eyed ones.'
In the <s>Mandākrāntā</s> meter, for example —
'The arm of <s>Śārṅgin</s> (<s>Viṣṇu</s>), difficult to behold, tawny-hued like the peacock's crest.'

children.text: dhātu-nāmabhāgapadagrahaṇāt tadbhāgātiriktabhede na bhavati yatibhraṣṭatvam / yathā mandākrāntāyām ----
children.translated_text: Because [the sūtra] specifies 'verbal root portion' and 'nominal portion,' when the split occurs in a part other than these, there is no faulty caesura. For example, in the <s>Mandākrāntā</s> —
'The fresh awakening of beautiful women causes beauty to blossom like flowers.'
In the <s>Śikharīṇī</s> meter, for example —
'Wakeful, at the dark edges, with the hissing sounds of the lower lip.'

children.text: svarasandhyakṛta iti vacanāt svarasandhikṛte bhede na doṣaḥ / yathā
children.translated_text: Because [the sūtra says] 'caused by vowel <s>sandhi</s>,' when the split is caused by vowel <s>sandhi</s>, there is no fault. For example —
'The gaze of beautiful women, somewhat languid with emotion, straightforward.'
The fault of caesura is not separate from the fault of meter, since meter consists of caesura. // VKal_2,2.5 //

children.text: vṛttadoṣāt pṛthag yatidoṣo na vaktavyaḥ / vṛttasya yatyātmakatvāt //5//
children.translated_text: The fault of caesura should not be stated separately from the fault of meter, since meter consists of caesura. //5//

children.text: yatyātmakaṃ hi vṛttamiti bhinnavṛtta eva yatibhraṣṭasyāntarbhāvānna pṛthaggrahaṇaṃ kāryamata āha ----
children.translated_text: Since meter consists of caesura, the fault of caesura is included within broken meter, and therefore need not be stated separately. Hence he says —
No, because the definitions are distinct. // VKal_2,2.6 //

children.text: nāyaṃ doṣaḥ lakṣaṇo lakṣaṇasya pṛthaktvāt / anyaddhi lakṣaṇaṃ vṛttasyānyacca yateḥ / gurulaghuniyamātmakaṃ vṛttam / virāmātmikā ca yatiriti //6//
children.translated_text: This is not a fault, because the definitions are distinct. The definition of meter is one thing, and that of caesura is another. Meter consists of the regulation of heavy and light syllables, while caesura consists of pauses. //6//
A malformed word-junction is called <s>visandhi</s> (bad conjunction). // VKal_2,2.7 //

children.text: padānāṃ sandhiḥ padasandhiḥ / sa ca svarasamavāyarūpaḥ pratyāsattimātrārūpo vā / sa virūpo yasminniti vigrahaḥ //7//
children.translated_text: The conjunction of words is <s>padasandhi</s> (word-junction). It may take the form of vowel combination or of mere proximity. That in which it is malformed — thus is the analysis. //7//
The malformation of word-junction consists of disjunction, vulgarity, and harshness. // VKal_2,2.8 //
Disjunction means separation, i.e., roughness. Disjunction, for example —
'By this mountain wind, in this mountain gorge,'

children.text: kamale iva locane ime anuvadhnāti vilāsapaddhatiḥ /
children.translated_text: 'like lotuses, these eyes follow the path of grace.'
'Faces adorned with flowing curls shine forth.'
Vulgarity, for example —
'This dance, arranged by the semblance of a teacher, is a purgative.'
'The city shone with jackfruit-like great eunuch trees.'
'Eager for a verbal dispute, without oaths or gifts.'
Harshness, for example —
'Those trees, pregnant with budding blossoms, became heavy-bodied.'
Having thus described the faults of sentences, he proceeds to explain the faults of sentence-meaning —
Sentences that are pointless, tautological, ambiguous, improper, inconsistent in sequence, [violating] worldly or learned knowledge, or contradictory [are faulty]. // VKal_2,2.9 //
The connection is: sentences are faulty [in these ways]. //9//
He proceeds to explain them in order —
That whose prior and subsequent meanings contradict each other is <s>vyartha</s> (pointless). // VKal_2,2.10 //

children.text: vyāhatau pūrvottarāvarthau yasmiṃstadvyāhatapūrvottarārthaṃ vākyaṃ vyartham / yathā ----
children.translated_text: A sentence in which the prior and subsequent meanings are contradictory is called <s>vyartha</s> (pointless). For example —

children.text:
adyāpi smarati rasālasaṃ mano me
  mugdhāyāḥ smaracaturāṇi ceṣṭitāni /
children.translated_text: 'Even today my mind remembers the languid, love-expert gestures of the naive maiden.'

children.text: mugdhāyāḥ kathaṃ smaracaturāṇi ceṣṭitāni / tāni cet kathaṃ mugdhā ? atra pūrvottarayorarthayorvirodhād vyarthamiti //10//
children.translated_text: How can the gestures of a naive maiden be 'love-expert'? And if they are, how is she naive? Here, because of the contradiction between the prior and subsequent meanings, it is pointless. //10//
That which repeats already-stated meaning is <s>ekārtha</s> (tautological). // VKal_2,2.11 //
That in which the words repeat already-stated meanings — that is <s>ekārtha</s> (tautological). For example —
'Anxiety, delusion — O <s>Anaṅga</s> (Love-god)! — the sidelong glance of the beautiful-browed one causes [them].'

children.text: anaṅgaḥ śṛṅgāraḥ / tasya cintāmohātmakatvāccintāmohaśabdau prayuktāvuktārthau bhavataḥ / ekārthapadatvād vākyamekārthamityuktam //11//
children.translated_text: <s>Anaṅga</s> means erotic love. Since it is inherently characterized by anxiety and delusion, the words 'anxiety' and 'delusion' are redundant. Because the words repeat the same meaning, the sentence is called tautological. //11//
No — if a distinction is [conveyed], the tautology is not a fault. // VKal_2,2.12 //

children.text: na gatārtha duṣṭaṃ viśeṣaścet pratipādyaḥ syāt //12//
children.translated_text: It is not faulty as redundancy if a distinction is being conveyed. //12//
To explain that distinction, he says —
In [the compound] '<s>dhanurjyā</s>' (bowstring), the mention of '<s>dhanus</s>' (bow) is for the comprehension of the superimposition. // VKal_2,2.13 //

children.text: dhanurjyādhvanāvityatra jyāśabdenoktārthatve'pi dhanuḥśrutiḥ prayujyate / ārūḍheḥ pratipattyai / ārohaṇasya pratipattyartham / na hi dhanuḥśrutimantareṇa dhanuṣyārūḍhā jyā dhanurjyeti śakyaṃ pratipattum / yathā ----
children.translated_text: In '<s>dhanurjyā-dhvani</s>' (the sound of the bowstring), even though the word '<s>jyā</s>' (string) already conveys the meaning, the word '<s>dhanus</s>' (bow) is used for the comprehension of the superimposition — i.e., for understanding the mounting [of the string on the bow]. For without the mention of '<s>dhanus</s>,' one cannot understand that the string is mounted on the bow as '<s>dhanurjyā</s>.' For example —
'By your arm, marked with the calluses of the bowstring, it was made to resound.'

In [compounds like] '<s>karṇāvataṃsa</s>' (ear-ornament), '<s>śravaṇa-kuṇḍala</s>' (ear-ring), and '<s>śiraḥ-śekhara</s>' (head-crest), the mention of '<s>karṇa</s>' etc. is for [indicating] proximity. // VKal_2,2.14 //

children.text: karṇāvataṃsādiśabdeṣu karṇādīnāmavataṃsādipadairuktārthānāmapi nirdeśaḥ sannidheḥ pratipattyarthamiti sambandhaḥ / na hi karṇādiśabdanirdeśamantareṇa karṇādisannihitānāmavataṃsādīnāṃ śakyā pratipattiḥ kartumiti / yathā ----
children.translated_text: In words like '<s>karṇāvataṃsa</s>' and so on, the mention of '<s>karṇa</s>' (ear) etc., even though the meaning is already conveyed by the words '<s>avataṃsa</s>' (ornament) etc., is for comprehension of proximity. For without the mention of '<s>karṇa</s>' and the like, the ornaments and such, which are situated near the ear etc., cannot be comprehended. For example —
'In the swaying movements of graceful women, the ear-ornaments exhibit trembling.'
'The playfully swaying ear-rings descend.'
'Those crowned with garlands, buzzing with bees, arrived swiftly.'
In the word '<s>muktāhāra</s>' (pearl-necklace), the word '<s>muktā</s>' (pearl) is for [indicating] purity. // VKal_2,2.15 //

children.text: muktāhāraśabde muktāśabdo hāraśabdenaiva gatārthaḥ prayujyate , śuddheḥ pratipattyarthamiti saṃbandhaḥ / śuddhānāmanyaratnairamiśritānāṃ hāro muktahāraḥ / yathā ----
children.translated_text: In the word '<s>muktāhāra</s>,' the word '<s>muktā</s>' (pearl), though its meaning is already conveyed by '<s>hāra</s>' (necklace), is used for comprehension of purity — i.e., the connection is: for understanding that the necklace is of pure pearls, unmixed with other gems. For example —
'Through the manifestations of the tumultuous embrace of the lord of her life,
the pair of breasts, shining with a pearl-necklace, seems to laugh.'
In the word '<s>puṣpamālā</s>' (flower-garland), the word '<s>puṣpa</s>' (flower) is for [indicating] excellence. // VKal_2,2.16 //

children.text: puṣpamālāśabde mālāśabdenaiva gatārthaṃ puṣpapadaṃ prayujyate / utkarṣasya pratipattyarthamiti / utkṛṣṭānāṃ puṣpāṇāṃ mālā puṣpamāleti yathā ----
children.translated_text: In the word '<s>puṣpamālā</s>' (flower-garland), the word '<s>puṣpa</s>' (flower) is used even though its meaning is already conveyed by the word '<s>mālā</s>' (garland) alone — for the purpose of indicating excellence. A garland of excellent flowers is '<s>puṣpamālā</s>.' As for example —

children.text: prāyaśaḥ puṣpamāleva kanyā sā kaṃ na lobhayet /
children.translated_text: That maiden, mostly like a flower-garland — whom would she not attract?

children.text: nanu mālāśabdo'nyatrāpi dṛśyate / yathā , ratnamālā , śabdamāleti / satyam / sa tāvadupacaritasya prayogaḥ / nirupapado hi mālāśabdaḥ puṣparacanāviśeṣamevābhidhatta iti //16//
children.translated_text: Now, the word '<s>mālā</s>' is seen used elsewhere too, as in '<s>ratnamālā</s>' (gem-garland), '<s>śabdamālā</s>' (word-garland). True. But that usage is figurative. For the word '<s>mālā</s>' without a qualifier denotes specifically an arrangement of flowers. // 16 //
In the word '<s>karikalabha</s>' (elephant-calf), the word '<s>kari</s>' (elephant) [is used] for indicating resemblance. // VKal_2,2.17 //

children.text: karikalabhaśabde kariśabdaḥ kalabhenaiva gatārthaḥ prayujyate ---- tādrūpyasya pratipattyarthamiti / karī prauḍhakuñjaraḥ / tadrūpaḥ kalabhaḥ karikalabha iti / yathā ----
children.translated_text: In the word '<s>karikalabha</s>' (elephant-calf), the word '<s>kari</s>' (elephant), whose meaning is already conveyed by '<s>kalabha</s>' (calf) alone, is used — for the purpose of indicating resemblance. '<s>Kari</s>' means a mature elephant. A calf resembling it is a '<s>karikalabha</s>.' As for example —
Abandon, O elephant-calf, the bond of affection for the she-elephant!
And [the same applies] for the qualifier. // VKal_2,2.18 //
The use of a word whose meaning is already expressed, for the purpose of indicating a distinction as a qualifier. As for example —
He spoke sweet speech, adorned with clear syllables.
This [applies] to those [words] that are [actually] used. // VKal_2,2.19 //

children.text: tadidamuktaṃ prayukteṣu , nāprayukteṣu / na hi , bhavati yathā ----

children.translated_text: '<s>śravaṇakuṇḍala</s>' (ear-earring).
Similarly —
'<s>nitambakāñcī</s>' (hip-girdle).
And also not —
'<s>karikalabha</s>' (elephant-calf).
Likewise —
'<s>uṣṭrakalabha</s>' (camel-calf).
And also not. Here is a verse —
This has been stated for words that are [actually] used, not for those that are not used. For it does not hold, as in the case of —
In words like '<s>karṇāvataṃsa</s>' (ear-ornament) and the like, the element '<s>karṇa</s>' (ear) and such is constructed
For the purpose of indicating the location of well-established things — this is the justification.
<s>Saṃśayakṛt</s> (doubt-creating) is <s>saṃdigdha</s> (ambiguous). // VKal_2,2.20 //

children.text: yadvākyaṃ sādhāraṇānāṃ dharmāṇāṃ śruteviṃśiṣṭānāṃ vā śruteḥ saṃśayaṃ karoti tat saṃśayakṛt sandigdhamiti / yathā ----
children.translated_text: That sentence which creates doubt, either from the hearing of common properties or from the hearing of distinctive ones, is called <s>saṃśayakṛt</s> (doubt-creating), that is, <s>saṃdigdha</s> (ambiguous). As for example —
That great soul, by the force of fate, attained a great position.

children.text: kiṃ bhāgyavaśānmahāpadamupāgataḥ , āhosvidabhāgyavaśānmahatīmāpadamiti saṃśayakṛd vākyaṃ , prakaraṇādyabhāve satīti //20//
children.translated_text: Whether 'by the force of [good] fate he attained a great position,' or 'by the force of [ill] fate he encountered a great calamity' — the sentence creates doubt, in the absence of contextual indication and the like. // 20 //
That in which the meaning is fabricated by <s>māyā</s> (illusion) and the like is improperly used. // VKal_2,2.21 //
That in which the meaning is fabricated by <s>māyā</s> and such devices is called improperly used. The examples of this are few. // 21 //
That which lacks the proper sequence of meaning is <s>apakrama</s> (disordered). // VKal_2,2.22 //

children.text: uddeśotānāmanuddeśitānāṃ ca kramaḥ sambandhaḥ / tena vihīno'rtho yasmiṃstatkramahīnārthamapakramam / yathā ----
children.translated_text: The sequence (<s>krama</s>) is the connection between those enumerated and those subsequently specified. That in which the meaning is devoid of this sequence is <s>kramahīnārtha</s> (disordered in meaning), that is, <s>apakrama</s> (disordered). As for example —
Your fame and valor are equal to those of the sun and moon.

children.text: atra kīrtiścandramasastulyā / pratāpaḥ sūryasya tulyaḥ / sūryasya pūrvanipātādakramaḥ / athavā pradhānasyārthasya nirdeśaḥ kramaḥ / tena vihīno'rtho yasmiṃstadapakramam / yathā ----
children.translated_text: Here, fame corresponds to the moon and valor to the sun. But since the sun is mentioned first, the sequence is disordered. Alternatively, <s>krama</s> (order) is the indication of the principal meaning. That in which the meaning is devoid of this is <s>apakrama</s> (disordered). As for example —
Give him a horse and then an intoxicated elephant.
Those whose meanings are contradicted by place, time, and nature are contradicted by common experience. // VKal_2,2.23 //

children.text: deśakālasvabhāvairviruddho'rtho yeṣu tāni deśakālasvabhāvaviruddhārthāni vākyāni lokaviruddhāni / arthadvāreṇa lokaviruddhatvaṃ vākyānām / deśaviruddhaṃ yathā ----
children.translated_text: Those sentences whose meanings are contradicted by place, time, and nature are said to be contradicted by common experience (<s>lokaviruddha</s>). The contradiction of sentences is through the medium of meaning. Contradicted by place, as for example —
In <s>Sauvīra</s> there is a city called <s>Madhurā</s>, well-known,
Whose surrounding lands are rich with walnut and coconut trees.
Contradicted by time, as for example —
The forest, smiling with <s>kadamba</s> blossoms, shone in spring.
Contradicted by nature, as for example —

children.text: mattālimaṅkhamukharāsu ca mañjarīṣu saptacchadasya taratīva śaransukhaśrīḥ /
children.translated_text: In the flower-clusters of the <s>saptacchada</s> tree, resonant with the humming of intoxicated bees, the beauty of autumn seems to surpass [all].

children.text: saptacchadasya stavakā bhavanti , na mañjarya iti svabhāvaviruddham / tathā ----
children.translated_text: The <s>saptacchada</s> tree bears clusters, not flower-spikes — thus this is contradicted by nature. Similarly —
The bud-sheath was so much pressed by the bee

children.text: yathā goṣpadapūraṃ hi vavarṣa bahulaṃ madhu //
children.translated_text: That it rained copious honey filling a cow's hoof-print.
Such an abundance of nectar from a single bud is contradicted by nature. // 23 //
Those whose meanings are contradicted by the sciences of arts and the four aims of life are contradicted by learning. // VKal_2,2.24 //

children.text: kalāśāstraiścaturvargaśāstraiśca viruddho'rtho yeṣu tāni kalācaturvargaśāstraviruddhārthāni vākyāni vidyāviruddhāni / vākyānāṃ virodho'rthadvārakaḥ / kalāśāstraviruddhaṃ yathā ----
children.translated_text: Those sentences whose meanings are contradicted by the sciences of arts and by the sciences of the four aims of life are said to be contradicted by learning (<s>vidyāviruddha</s>). The contradiction of sentences is through the medium of meaning. Contradicted by the science of arts, as for example —
O <s>Kāliṅga</s>, this leaf has been drawn by experts in leaf-design, with the tip-thorns not meeting.

children.text: kālinṅgaṃ patitakoṭikaṇṭakāgramiti patravidāmāmnāyaḥ / tadviruddhatvāt kalāśāstraviruddham / evaṃ kalāntareṣvapi virodho'bhyūhyaḥ / caturvargaśāstraviruddhāni tūdāhniyante ----
children.translated_text: The traditional teaching of leaf-experts is that the <s>kāliṅga</s> leaf has tip-thorns that meet. Since it contradicts that, it is contradicted by the science of arts. In the same way, contradiction with other arts should be inferred. Examples contradicted by the sciences of the four aims of life are now cited —
The conquest of the earth by kings has the full enjoyment of pleasures as its fruit.
The traditional teaching is that the conquest of the earth by kings has <s>dharma</s> (righteousness) as its fruit, or the fruit of sacrifices such as the <s>Aśvamedha</s>.
Since it contradicts that, this sentence has a meaning contradicted by the science of <s>dharma</s> (law).
Are enemies conquered by pride alone? What need is there for the glory of statecraft?

children.text: dvipajjayasya nayamūlatvaṃ sthitaṃ daṇḍanītau / tadvirodhādarthaśāstraviruddha vākyamiti /
children.translated_text: The science of statecraft (<s>Daṇḍanīti</s>) establishes that the conquest of enemies is rooted in statecraft. Since it contradicts that, this is a sentence contradicted by the science of <s>artha</s> (polity).
I remember the face languid with the fatigue of love-play, with the upper lip sanctified by tooth-marks.
The proper places for kissing, scratching, and biting are the upper lip when turned inward, the corner of the eye, and so forth —

children.text: iti kāmaśāstre sthitam / tadvirodhāt kāmaśāstraviruddhārthaṃ vākyamiti
children.translated_text: Thus is established in the science of <s>kāma</s> (love). Since it contradicts that, this is a sentence with a meaning contradicted by the science of <s>kāma</s>.
Liberation comes from devotion to the deity, not from the wealth of knowledge of truth.

children.text:
etasyārthasya mokṣaśāstre sthitatvāttadviruddhārtham /
ete vākyavākyārthadoṣāstyāgāya jñātavyāḥ / ye tvanye śabdārthadoṣāḥ sūkṣmāste guṇavivecane lakṣyante / upamādoṣāścopamāvicāra iti //24//
children.translated_text: Since this meaning is established in the science of <s>mokṣa</s> (liberation) [to be otherwise], it has a contradictory meaning. These are the faults of sentences and sentence-meanings, to be known for the purpose of avoidance. Those other faults of words and meanings that are subtle are indicated in the discussion of virtues. And the faults of simile are [discussed] in the examination of simile. // 24 //

children.text: iti śrīkāvyālaṅkārasūtravṛttau doṣadarśane dvitīye'dhikaraṇe dvitīyo'dhyāyaḥ / vākyavākyārthadoṣavibhāgaḥ //2-2//
children.translated_text: Thus ends the second chapter of the second section on the examination of faults in the <s>Kāvyālaṅkārasūtravṛtti</s> — the division of faults of sentences and sentence-meanings. // 2-2 //
Thus is completed the second section, the examination of faults. // 2 //
The first chapter of the third section.

children.text: yadviparyayātmāno doṣāstān guṇān vicārayituṃ guṇavivecanamadhikaraṇamārabhyate / tatraujaḥprasādādayo guṇā yamakopamādayastvalaṅkārā iti sthitiḥ kāvyavidām / teṣāṃ kiṃ bhedanibandhanamityāha ----
children.translated_text: In order to discuss the virtues (<s>guṇas</s>), which are the opposites of the faults, the third section on the examination of virtues is commenced. Therein, <s>ojas</s> (vigor), <s>prasāda</s> (clarity), and the like are virtues, while <s>yamaka</s> (rhyme), <s>upamā</s> (simile), and the like are ornaments — such is the established view of the authorities on poetry. To state what is the basis of their distinction —
The properties that create the beauty of poetry are the virtues (<s>guṇas</s>). // VKal_3,1.1 //

children.text: ye khalu śabdārthayordharmāḥ kāvyaśobhāṃ kurvanti te guṇāḥ / te caujaḥprasādayaḥ / na yamakopamādayaḥ / kauvalyena teṣāmakāvyaśobhākaratvāt / ojaḥprasādādīnāṃ tu kevalānāmasti kāvyaśobhākaratvamiti //1//
children.translated_text: Those properties of words and meanings that create the beauty of poetry are the virtues (<s>guṇas</s>). These are <s>ojas</s> (vigor), <s>prasāda</s> (clarity), and so forth — not <s>yamaka</s> (rhyme), <s>upamā</s> (simile), and the like. Because the latter alone do not create poetic beauty. But <s>ojas</s>, <s>prasāda</s>, and the rest, even by themselves, do create poetic beauty. // 1 //
The causes of the enhancement of that [beauty] are the ornaments (<s>alaṅkāras</s>). // VKal_3,1.2 //

children.text: tasyāḥ kāvyaśobhāyā atiśayastadatiśayastasya hetavaḥ / {tu}śabdo vyatireke / alaṅkārāśca yamakopamādayaḥ / atra ślokau ----
children.translated_text: The causes of the enhancement of that poetic beauty — that is what is meant by 'the causes of its enhancement.' The word 'tu' (but) indicates contrast. The ornaments are <s>yamaka</s> (rhyme), <s>upamā</s> (simile), and the like. Here are two verses —
Poetry, like the figure of a young woman, delights when endowed with pure virtues, and even more so
When intimately adorned with continuous inventive applications of ornaments.

children.text: yadi bhavati vacaścyutaṃ guṇebhyo vapuriva yauvanavandhyamaṅganāyāḥ /
children.translated_text: If speech is devoid of virtues, like the body of a maiden bereft of youth,
Even ornaments dear to people inevitably take on the character of wretchedness.
The former [i.e., the virtues] are permanent. // VKal_3,1.3 //
The former, the virtues, are permanent — because without them, poetic beauty is impossible. // 3 //
Having thus shown the distinction between virtues and ornaments, in order to define the virtues of words, he says —

<s>Ojas</s> (vigor), <s>prasāda</s> (clarity), <s>śleṣa</s> (cohesion), <s>samatā</s> (evenness), <s>samādhi</s> (balance), <s>mādhurya</s> (sweetness), <s>saukumārya</s> (delicacy), <s>udāratā</s> (nobility), <s>arthavyakti</s> (clarity of meaning), and <s>kānti</s> (charm) are the virtues of composition. // VKal_3,1.4 //

children.text: bandhaḥ padaracanā , tasya guṇaḥ bandhaguṇāḥ ojaḥprabhṛtayaḥ //4//
children.translated_text: <s>Bandha</s> (composition) is the arrangement of words; its virtues (<s>guṇas</s>) are the virtues of composition, beginning with <s>ojas</s> (vigor). // 4 //
To demonstrate these in order, he says —
Compact composition is <s>ojas</s> (vigor). // VKal_3,1.5 //
As for example —
They make the flower-clusters, with their honey disturbed, dance.
But not —
They make the flower-clusters, with streams of nectar displaced, sway.
Looseness is <s>prasāda</s> (clarity). // VKal_3,1.6 //
The looseness, that is, the relaxed quality of the composition, is <s>prasāda</s> (clarity). // 6 //

children.text: nanvayamojoviparyayātmā doṣa , tat kathaṃ guṇa ityāha ----
children.translated_text: Now, this being the opposite of <s>ojas</s> (vigor) is a fault — how then is it a virtue? To this he replies —
It is a virtue because of its confluence [with ojas]. // VKal_3,1.7 //
<s>Prasāda</s> (clarity) is a virtue because of its confluence with <s>ojas</s> (vigor). // 7 //

children.text: na śuddhaḥ // VKal_3,1.8 [k: not in sutra] //
children.translated_text: But in its pure form, it is not [a virtue]. // VKal_3,1.8 //
In its pure form, however, it is indeed a fault. // 8 //

children.text: nanu viruddhayorojaḥprasādayoḥ kathaṃ saṃplava ityata āha ----
children.translated_text: Now, how can there be a confluence of <s>ojas</s> and <s>prasāda</s>, which are opposites? To this he replies —
That [confluence], however, is established by experience. // VKal_3,1.9 //

children.text: sa tu saṃplavastvanubhavasiddhaḥ / tadvidāṃ ratnādiviśeṣavat / atra ślokaḥ ----
children.translated_text: That confluence is established by experience, like the knowledge of particular gems and the like by connoisseurs. Here is a verse —
In things that are pathetically beautiful to behold, there is a confluence of pleasure and pain;
Just as that is established through experience, so too is the confluence of <s>ojas</s> (vigor) and <s>prasāda</s> (clarity).
And also equality and superiority. // VKal_3,1.10 //
Equality and superiority pertain to <s>ojas</s> (vigor) and <s>prasāda</s> (clarity) alone. Equality, as for example —

children.text:
atha sa viṣayavyāvṛttātmā yathāvidhi sūnave
  nṛpatikakudaṃ datvā yūne sitātapavāraṇam //
children.translated_text: Then he, his mind withdrawn from sense-objects, having duly given to his son the royal parasol, the white umbrella, while still young —
(<s>Raghuvaṃśa</s> 3.70)
Sometimes <s>ojas</s> (vigor) is superior to <s>prasāda</s> (clarity). As for example —
It rises to the sky, becoming comparable to the fruit of the <s>bhallātaka</s> tree.
Sometimes <s>prasāda</s> (clarity) is superior to <s>ojas</s> (vigor). As for example —

children.text:
kusumaśayanaṃ na pratyayaṃ na candramarīcayo
  na ca malayajaṃ sarvāṅgīṇaṃ na vā maṇiyaṣṭayaḥ //
children.translated_text: Neither a bed of flowers is agreeable, nor the rays of the moon, nor full-body application of sandalwood, nor jeweled staffs.
Smoothness is <s>śleṣa</s> (cohesion). // VKal_3,1.11 //

children.text: masṛṇatvaṃ nāma yasmin santi bahūnyapi padānyekavadbhāsante / yathā ----
children.translated_text: Smoothness means that in which, even though there are many words, they appear as one. As for example —

children.text: astyuttarasyāṃ diśi devatātmā himālayo nāma nagādhirājaḥ /
children.translated_text: In the northern direction there is a king of mountains, divine in nature, called <s>Himālaya</s>.
(<s>Kumārasaṃbhava</s> 1.1)
But not —
A Brahmanical thread on the chest —
The sweet songs of the female bee,
The sky filled with lightning,
And so on.
But <s>śleṣa</s> (cohesion) occurs thus —
A Brahmanical thread on the chest,
The charming songs of the female bee,
The sky tangled with lightning,
And so on.
Non-deviation from the path is <s>samatā</s> (evenness). // VKal_3,1.12 //

children.text: mārgasyābhedo mārgābhedaḥ samatā / yena mārgeṇopakramastasyātyāga ityarthaḥ / śloke prabandhe ceti pūrvoktamudāharaṇam / viparyayastu yathā ----
children.translated_text: Non-deviation from the path is <s>samatā</s> (evenness). The meaning is: not abandoning the manner in which one has begun. The example previously cited applies to both verse and continuous composition. The opposite, as for example —

children.text: prasīda caṇḍi ! tyaja manyumañjasā janastavāyaṃ purataḥ kṛtāñjaliḥ /
children.translated_text: Be gracious, O fierce one! Abandon your anger immediately — this person stands before you with palms joined.
Why do you sit with your large trembling breasts, your face devoid of charm, for what purpose?
The sequence of rising and falling is <s>samādhi</s> (balance). // VKal_3,1.13 //

children.text: ārohāvarohayoḥ krama ārohāvarohakramaḥ samādhiḥ parihāraḥ / ārohasyāvarohe sati parihāraḥ , avarohasya vārohe satīti / tatrārphapūrvako'varoho yathā ----
children.translated_text: The sequence of rising and falling, called <s>samādhi</s> (balance), is the counterbalancing. When there is a fall after a rise, there is counterbalancing; or when there is a rise after a fall. Among these, a fall preceded by a rise, as for example —

children.text: narāḥ śīlabhraṣṭā vyasana iva majjanti taravaḥ /
children.translated_text: People who have fallen from good conduct sink as if into a disaster, like trees.

children.text: ārohasya kramo'varohasya ca krama ārohāvarohakramaḥ / krameṇārohaṇamavarohaṇaṃ ceti kecit / yathā ----
children.translated_text: The sequence of rise and of fall is the sequence of rising and falling. Some explain it as the gradual ascent and descent. As for example —
The dwelling on the celestial <s>Gaṅgā</s>, on the slopes of the snow-mountain, is glorious.
It is not a separate [virtue], because rising and falling are of the nature of <s>ojas</s> (vigor) and <s>prasāda</s> (clarity). // VKal_3,1.14 //

children.text: na pṛthaksamādhirguṇaḥ ārohāvarohayorojaḥprasādarūpatvāt / pjorūpaścārohaḥ prasādarūpaścāvaroha iti //14//
children.translated_text: <s>Samādhi</s> (balance) is not a separate virtue, because rising and falling are of the nature of <s>ojas</s> (vigor) and <s>prasāda</s> (clarity) respectively. The rise is of the nature of <s>ojas</s>, and the fall is of the nature of <s>prasāda</s>. // 14 //
No, because they are not intermixed. // VKal_3,1.15 //
The nature of <s>ojas</s> (vigor) and <s>prasāda</s> (clarity) belongs to <s>āroha</s> (ascent) and <s>avaroha</s> (descent) —
objection:

children.text: tanna / sampṛktatvāt[k: asampṛktatvāt] / sampṛktau khalvojaḥprasādau nadīveṇikāvad vahataḥ //15//
children.translated_text: that is not so, because of their being intermingled. Indeed, when intermingled, <s>ojas</s> and <s>prasāda</s> flow together like the confluence of two rivers. //15//
What was stated [above] —
And because of the absence of invariable concomitance. // VKal_3,1.16 //
And this is not an invariable rule — [namely] that <s>ojas</s> corresponds to ascent and <s>prasāda</s> to descent. //16//
If [you say that] the intense states of <s>ojas</s> and <s>prasāda</s> are those [ascent and descent], that is [merely] a concession. // VKal_3,1.17 //

children.text: ojaḥprasādayoḥ kvacidbhāge tīvrāvasthāyāmāroho'varohaścetyevaṃ[k: tīvrāvasthā / sā cāroho'varohākhyetyevaṃ] cenmanyase , abhyupagamaḥ ---- na vipratipattiḥ //17//
children.translated_text: If you think that the intense state of <s>ojas</s> and <s>prasāda</s> in some portion constitutes ascent and descent respectively, then this is merely a concession — not a disagreement. //17//
Because those two depend on a distinguishing factor. // VKal_3,1.18 //
That distinguishing factor is constituted by another quality. //18//
The cause of ascent and descent is explained as <s>samādhi</s> (concentration). // VKal_3,1.19 //
The sequence of ascent and descent should be explained as <s>samādhi</s> by means of a secondary (figurative) usage. //19//
Or, for the purpose of [explaining] the arrangement of sequence. // VKal_3,1.20 //
[as the sūtra says:] 'They are not properties of the word-arrangement, because [they are] not observed everywhere'
(3-1-28) — thus we shall state later. //20//
[This means] treating them separately. And that it is a property of the arrangement of words is not possible —
The separateness of words is <s>mādhurya</s> (sweetness). // VKal_3,1.21 //

children.text: bandhasya pṛthakpadatvaṃ yat tanmādhuryam pṛthakpadāni yasya sa pṛthakpadaḥ / tasya bhāvaḥ pṛthakpadatvam / samāsadairdhyanivṛttiparaṃ caitat /
children.translated_text: The separateness of words in the composition — that is <s>mādhurya</s> (sweetness). 'Separate-worded' means that whose words are separate; its abstract quality is 'separateness of words.' And this refers to the avoidance of excessive length of compounds.
Non-harshness is <s>saukumārya</s> (delicacy). // VKal_3,1.22 //

children.text: bandhasyājaraṭhatvamapāruṣyaṃ yat yat saukumāryam / pūrvoktamudāharaṇam / viparyayastu yathā ----
children.translated_text: The non-harshness of the composition, that is, the absence of roughness, is <s>saukumārya</s> (delicacy). The previously stated example [applies]. The contrary, however, is as follows —

children.text:
nidānaṃ nirdvaitaṃ priyajanasadṛktvavyavasitiḥ
  sudhāsekaploṣau phalamapi viruddhaṃ mama hṛdi /
